## The Daily Body Count

Every single day:

- **150,000 people stop existing**
- **130,000 from disease** (diseases are very effective at their job)
- **80,000 were preventable [@53-percent-preventable-deaths]** (the technology existed; nobody reached for it)
- **13,700 are children [@5-million-annual-child-deaths]** (which matters if you believe children should continue existing)

That's fifty 9/11s. Every. Single. Day.

After the first 9/11, America invaded two countries and spent $2 trillion. After the fifty daily 9/11s, humanity shrugs and checks Instagram.

Every hour: **6,250 deaths**. Every minute: **104 deaths**. Every second: **1.7 deaths**.

If you took everyone in a decent-sized stadium and deleted them, that's one day. Then do it again tomorrow. And the day after that. Forever. You'd run out of stadiums before you'd run out of corpses, which seems like poor urban planning.

That's the body count. Now let's talk about the bill.

## The Financial Cost

While you read this sentence, disease just deleted $12.7 million of human potential from existence.

By the time you finish this paragraph, $60 million more will evaporate into cancer treatments, heart surgeries, and funeral expenses. Also Dave from accounting's weird rash, but that's probably unrelated.

Humanity hemorrhages **{{< var global_disease_economic_burden_annual >}} annually** [@disease-economic-burden-109t] to diseases that are basically just engineering problems with meat robots.

That's more than the entire global economy. Every year. You lose more money to disease than you make doing everything else combined. It's like running a lemonade stand that costs more in lemons than the entire GDP of Earth.

"Wait," you say, "global GDP is only $101 trillion [@global-gdp]. How can we lose more than everything that exists?"

Because economists forgot to include the dying part. For centuries, economics measured productivity without accounting for the people who stopped being productive on account of being dead. This is like calculating the cost of a plane crash without including the plane, the passengers, or the fact that they were going somewhere.

## The Actual Bill (Economist-Approved Misery Accounting)

Here's what disease actually costs, translated from economist-speak into human language:

| What We're Losing | What This Actually Means | Annual Cost |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Direct cash costs** | Paying doctors to Google your symptoms in a room that costs $500/hour, plus the spreadsheets sick people never make | {{< var global_disease_total_market_cost_annual >}} [@disease-economic-burden-109t] |
| **What the lost life is actually worth (DALYs)** | Dead people contribute zero to the economy (economists finally noticed). This is the real number; the cash above is just the part with receipts | {{< var global_disease_economic_burden_annual >}} [@ihme-gbd-2019] |
| **TOTAL DISASTER** | **More money than exists on Earth** | **{{< var global_disease_economic_burden_annual >}}** [@disease-economic-burden-109t] |

Let me explain that last one, because it's where the real horror lives.
## How to Measure Suffering Without Feeling Feelings (The DALY)

DALY stands for "Disability-Adjusted Life Year." That's economist-speak for "quantifying human misery without having to look people in the eye."

![DALYs measure healthy years lost. Dying at 30 instead of 80 loses 50 years. Living 50 years in a wheelchair at 50% capacity loses 25 years. The math is simple. Fixing it is apparently hard.](/assets/images/cost-of-disease/cost-of-disease-section-how-to-measure-suffering-without-feeling-feelings-the-daly-bw-academic.jpg)

One DALY = One year of healthy human life, deleted.

Die at 40 instead of 80?
That's 40 DALYs.
Spend 10 years severely depressed?
That's 5 DALYs (economists calculated that being miserable counts as being half-dead, which is oddly accurate).

The entire human species combined? **{{< var global_annual_daly_burden_nounit >}} DALYs annually [@ihme-gbd-2019]**. That's {{< var global_annual_daly_burden_nounit >}} years of human potential, dissolving annually into medical bills and funeral expenses.

### What the WHO Thinks You're Worth (Less Than a Tesla)

The World Health Organization decided one year of human life is worth 1-3 times GDP per capita [@who-choice-daly-value]. They made this calculation sober, which is surprising.

Let's use 3x GDP per capita. We're optimists who think humans are worth at least three years of their economic output. This is the most generous estimate bureaucrats could manage, and it's still less than a luxury sedan.

The math is simple and horrifying:

- Value per healthy year: {{< var standard_economic_qaly_value_usd >}} (less than a Tesla, apparently)
- Total DALYs lost annually: {{< var global_annual_daly_burden_nounit >}} years, about 93% of them eventually avoidable

Multiply the avoidable years by the value:

{{< var global_disease_economic_burden_annual_latex >}}

That's {{< var global_disease_economic_burden_annual >}} of human potential. We flush it annually down the toilet labeled "diseases we haven't cured yet because the money went to bombs."

## Let's Break Down This Apocalypse By Time Unit

{{< var global_disease_economic_burden_annual >}} annually breaks down to:

- **$1.1 trillion EVERY DAY** (more than most countries make in a year)
- **$45.7 billion EVERY HOUR** (enough to fund a mid-size cancer research institute)
- **$761 million EVERY MINUTE** (more than most lottery jackpots)
- **$12.7 million EVERY SECOND** (a new Tesla Roadster worth of human potential, gone, every second, forever)

By the time you finish this chapter (about 10 minutes), disease will have cost humanity more than the entire Apollo moon program. We went to the moon for less than one chapter's worth of disease costs.
The math is, as your children say, not mathing.

Here's what's killing people while you read about what's killing people:

| Heart Disease | 20 million [@death-causes-vs-fear] | 54,800 | 500 |

| **TOTAL** | **{{< var global_annual_deaths_curable_diseases_nounit >}} [@who-daily-deaths]** | **150,000** | **1,370** |

1,370 humans will permanently stop existing while you read this chapter. That's five 747s crashing. Every 10 minutes. Forever. If this happened to actual planes, you'd ground all flights within an hour and the 24-hour news cycle would collapse from overuse. But because it's disease, you call it "natural causes" and go back to arguing about parking.

While you're busy testing 0.000003% of potential cures:

- **10 million people annually [@amr-10m-2050]** will die from antimicrobial resistance by 2050 (bacteria evolved faster than we did, which is embarrassing)
- **600,000 people annually [@malaria-deaths-600k-annually]** die from malaria (mosquitoes: 600,000, humanity: 0)
- **10.4 million people annually [@cancer-deaths-10m-annually]** die from cancer (your own cells killing you because they forgot how to die). That's more than the population of Sweden. Sweden is being eliminated by cancer every twelve months and nobody has declared war on it. Well, Nixon did, in 1971. Cancer won.
- **20 million people annually [@death-causes-vs-fear]** die from cardiovascular disease (hearts that gave up on humanity, can't blame them)

Each death represents:

- Someone's entire universe ending
- A grandmother who won't meet grandchildren
- A scientist who might have cured the thing that killed them
- $4 million in lost economic value (if we're being cold about it, which economists always are)
- Infinite sadness if you're the one dying, mild inconvenience if you're not

## Your Body Is Not Magic, It's Just Broken

Your body is a machine. Not mystical, not "in balance with the universe." A biological machine made of 37 trillion cells. And like all machines, it breaks.

**Machines can be fixed.**

Every disease is just a broken part: cancer is cells with broken stop buttons, Alzheimer's is broken garbage disposal in brain cells, aging is everything breaking at once very slowly (rude).

These don't get fixed because 99.999997% of the repair tools are untested. There are 166 billion possible molecules. Humanity has tried ~0.003% of them. That's like looking for your car keys by checking one pocket then giving up forever.

![Heart disease is like a clogged pipe. Cancer is like cells that forgot how to stop. Diabetes is like a broken thermostat. Everyone understands pipes. Nobody can fix the pipes inside them.](/assets/images/cost-of-disease/cost-of-disease-section-disease-mechanics-infographic-bw-academic.jpg)

## What This Actually Costs

The {{< var global_disease_economic_burden_annual >}} "Disease Tax" is optional. Not optional like "you can skip it," but optional like "it's not a law of physics, just a choice humanity keeps making."
It's the price of humanity being too slow to fix its own broken meat robots.

Every day you delay costs another **$1.1 trillion** in human potential dissolving into medical bills, funeral expenses, and GoFundMe campaigns. Meanwhile, politicians argue whether you can "afford" to test molecules.

### Your Priorities, Written in Your Budgets

- **Military budget:** Gets $7.4 billion daily [@sipri2024] to practice ending human life
- **Medical research:** Gets $185 million daily [@global-gov-med-research-spending] to practice extending it

That's a **40:1 ratio in favor of death over life.**

If aliens intercepted your budget spreadsheets, they'd conclude you're a death cult that occasionally dabbles in medicine as a hobby. (We have intercepted them. This is accurate.)

### The Future You're Paying For

Somewhere in the future, there's a Tuesday when:

- Cancer is a minor inconvenience like a cold
- Hearts are as repairable as carburetors
- Death is optional, not mandatory
- Aging is something that happened to your ancestors

Every day between now and that Tuesday costs you $1.1 trillion. That's the real invoice. The actual bill for choosing bombs over grandma's cancer treatment.

![Every day of military spending delays the cancer cure by another day. It's been delayed for 75 years now. The cancer is very patient.](/assets/images/cost-of-disease/cost-of-disease-section-the-future-you-re-paying-for-bw-academic.jpg)

The future is waiting. Humanity's just too busy building better ways to explode each other to notice. The explosions are very impressive, though. Full marks for spectacle.
